I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other threat items reflect hypervigilance and perceived danger (silence, being on guard at home), while memory and appraisal items center on intrusive, overwhelming captivity memories and beliefs that the world is dangerous or that she is 'going crazy.' Risk-taking points toward a different behavioral pattern that is not supported elsewhere, especially with Maladaptive Strategies absent and Threat not strongly linked outward in the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living
issues.explanation: 'Life Not Worth Living' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected appraisals, which otherwise focus on danger and loss of control ('world is dangerous,' 'going crazy'). It introduces a severe hopelessness/suicidal cognition not echoed in memory, threat, or strategy items. At PCL-5 53 severe symptoms are plausible, but this specific appraisal is insufficiently supported by the rest of the profile and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette:
Marisol had spent most of her adult life working as a paramedic in a large Latin American community in the United States, the kind of job that required her to move quickly, keep her voice steady, and be ready for whatever scene waited behind a door. At 66, married and close to retirement, she had expected the pace of her life to slow down. Instead, she found herself thinking more and more about one incident from years earlier, when she had been taken captive during a violent emergency call. She had gone in with a partner, expecting a rescue, and within minutes the situation had turned into hours of being trapped, watched, and unable to leave. What stayed with her was not only the fear of the people holding her, but the long stretches of silence between their movements and the sound of her own breathing as she tried not to draw attention to herself. She remembered the room’s stillness as something alive, as if the silence itself meant danger was close.

When Marisol first got home after that ordeal, her husband said she looked intact, but she felt as if something essential in her had been split off and left behind. In the months that followed, the memory did not sit in the past the way other memories did. It forced its way into her mind at odd moments, sometimes when she was washing dishes, sometimes while she was driving to work, sometimes without any obvious reminder at all. She would suddenly find herself back in that confined space, feeling the same pressure in her chest and the same helpless waiting, and when the memory took hold she became overwhelmed by emotion so quickly that she had to stop what she was doing. On some occasions she would stand frozen in the kitchen, hands wet, unable to continue until the wave passed. The memory also felt strangely unreal to her, so extreme and disconnected from ordinary life that she struggled to believe it had happened to her at all. At times she would say quietly to her husband that it sounded like the story of another person, not hers, as if her mind were resisting the fact that she had lived through it.

Over time, Marisol came to see the world differently. She had always known that emergencies could be unpredictable, but after the captivity she became certain that danger could erupt anywhere and that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. That sense of helplessness followed her into ordinary places. Even at home, where she had once felt most secure, she remained on guard. She would scan the front window after dark, listen to the hallway sounds in the apartment building, and feel uneasy if the house became too quiet. Unusual silence, which other people might have found restful, made her feel that something dangerous was about to happen. If the television went off or her husband was in another room and the house fell still, her body tensed before she could reason with herself.

Marisol also found herself checking behind her when she was outside, especially in parking lots or when walking from her car to a building. She frequently looked over her shoulder to make sure no one was following her, a habit that had become automatic enough that her husband noticed it before she did. At work, this vigilance made some parts of her job harder. As a paramedic, she still went to the station and did her shifts, but she felt less settled in the in-between moments: standing in a quiet ambulance bay, waiting in a corridor, hearing a dispatch pause before the next call. The silence between radio communications could tighten her stomach. She remained capable and professional, but the job no longer felt like it belonged to the same unshaken person she had once been.

What troubled Marisol most was how these reactions made her interpret herself. She had come to believe that her jumpiness and constant checking meant she was going crazy. She disliked saying this aloud, but the thought returned often enough that she treated it almost as a fact. In her mind, a reasonable person should have been able to put such an experience behind her. Instead she found herself living as though she were still waiting for something to happen, and that discrepancy frightened her. She did not want to be seen as fragile, especially after a career spent helping other people through their worst moments. Yet she also could not deny that the experience had changed how she moved through the world. She was now more careful in ways that narrowed her life: less comfortable walking alone, slower to relax in her own home, and more likely to sit near exits or keep watch on doorways.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was tired of feeling as though she had to brace herself for the next threat even in places that should have been safe. She told the therapist she wanted to understand why the memory still arrived with such force and why ordinary quiet could make her feel alarmed before anything had happened. More than anything, she hoped to stop feeling as if danger was always just behind her, and to believe again that she and her husband could share a home and a life without her body acting as though captivity were about to happen again.
